nodes.name: Douglas Fir
nodes.desc: A dominant tall conifer of the lower forests. Its seeds are eaten by Douglas squirrels, chickadees and other small animals.

nodes.name: Western hemlock
nodes.desc: Along with western red cedar and Douglas fir, it dominates the low, wet valleys of the park, where old-growth forest covers a large area.

nodes.name: Thimbleberry
nodes.desc: A soft-leaved shrub of forest openings. Its leaves and berries are eaten by deer, hares, bears and bumble bees.

nodes.name: Fireweed
nodes.desc: A tall wildflower that spreads quickly across burned or cleared ground and is browsed by mule deer.

nodes.name: Alpine heath & meadow plants
nodes.desc: Mountain heath, partridgefoot and other low plants of the subalpine meadows, which cover the slopes roughly between 4,000 and 7,000 feet.

nodes.name: Whitebark pine
nodes.desc: A high-elevation pine whose large seeds feed nutcrackers, squirrels and bears. Blister rust and pine beetles have killed many of the park trees.

nodes.name: Douglas squirrel
nodes.desc: Cuts and stores cones in middens and eats conifer seeds. Bears raid whitebark pine middens for seeds.

nodes.name: Mule deer
nodes.desc: A browser that eats wildflowers, shrubs and conifer foliage, and is a main prey of cougars. The park lists Columbia black-tailed deer, a mule deer form, as a common sight.

nodes.name: Snowshoe hare
nodes.desc: Browses shrubs and young plants through the year. It is the staple prey of the Canada lynx.

nodes.name: Mountain goat
nodes.desc: Grazes alpine and subalpine slopes on grasses, herbs, shrubs and twigs. Cougars are probably its main predator, with eagles taking kids.

nodes.name: Hoary marmot
nodes.desc: A big ground squirrel of alpine meadows that eats grasses and flowering plants, then hibernates through the long snowy winter.

nodes.name: American pika
nodes.desc: Gathers meadow plants into hay piles in rock slides. Sensitive to heat, so warming mountain slopes are a concern.

nodes.name: Clark's nutcracker
nodes.desc: The main disperser of whitebark pine. It buries thousands of seeds each year, and the ones it forgets can grow into new trees.

nodes.name: Canada lynx
nodes.desc: A snow-adapted cat reported in the park that specializes on snowshoe hares.

nodes.name: Golden eagle
nodes.desc: A bird of prey listed among the park raptors. It hunts marmots and hares in open country and can take goat kids.

nodes.name: Common raven
nodes.desc: A clever omnivore that scavenges carcasses such as deer and goats and also eats seeds and small animals.

nodes.name: Cougar
nodes.desc: A large cat whose main prey is deer and other hoofed animals. Likely the top predator of mountain goats.

nodes.name: American black bear
nodes.desc: An omnivore that eats berries, whitebark pine seeds raided from squirrel middens, and sometimes deer, goats and hares.

nodes.name: Rain & snowfall
nodes.desc: The west side gets far more precipitation than the east, with deep snowpacks of 10 to 25 feet at their early March peak in the mountains.

nodes.name: Snowpack & glaciers
nodes.desc: The park has about 312 glaciers. Melt feeds cold streams in late summer, but the ice is shrinking.

nodes.name: Wildfire
nodes.desc: Large natural fires are rare and come every few decades to centuries, and lightning fires are often allowed to burn.

nodes.name: Forest soil
nodes.desc: Holds the nutrients and moisture that the forests and meadows draw on.

nodes.name: Fungi, insects & bacteria
nodes.desc: Break down fallen logs, needles, carcasses and dung and return nutrients to the soil.
